questions.stem: A 35-year-old man attended for care. He was known to have HIV , HCV , and HBV infection related to previous intravenous drug use. He had previously been inconsistent in care but had completed a treatment program for his drug dependency 6 months and now attended regularly for follow up. Investigations: ALT 330 IU/L CD4 430 cells/μL HIV viral load: 90,000 copies/mL; no resistance on genotypic testing HBV sAg positive, eAg positive, cAb positive; HBV eAb negative HBV DNA: 22,000 IU/mL HCV IgG positive, genotype 1; HCV viral load 600,000 IU/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir alafenamide, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir In a patient co-infected with HBV and HIV , treatment should include tenofovir to cover both viruses. Only A and E include fully active antiretroviral regimens, and only E includes tenofovir. Although lamivudine has activity against HBV , resistance develops quickly. Regimen B would be unconventional and would cover HIV but has no HBV coverage, and ledipasvir alone will not treat HCV . Regimen D includes a single drug for HBV , HIV , and HCV . Both HIV and HCV require more than one active antiviral for efficacy. Given the risk of HBV reactivation with treatment of HCV , in the setting of all three infections, most would recommend controlling HIV and HBV first before starting HCV therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q20

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man was being treated for hepatitis C with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir. Investigations: HAV IgG positive HBV cAb positive, HBV sAg negative, HBV sAb 0 HBV DNA undetectable A B HCV IgG positive, HCV genotype 1a Liver biopsy showed grade 1 inflammation and stage 3 fibrosis with features of both chronic HCV and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Baseline Week 4 Week 11 ALT (IU/L) 170 35 2250 AST (IU/L) 289 32 2970 HCV viral load (IU/mL) 1,200,000 Undetectable Undetectable INR 1.8 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 7.2
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely reason for the worsening transaminases?
questions.explanation: Reactivation of HBV Reactivation of HBV in a patient with co-infection with HBV and HCV has been reported in patients being treated for HCV . A patient responding to HCV treatment who has a flare of hepatitis, but still with undetectable HCV viral loads, should be evaluated for HBV . Drug reaction is possible but rarely causes transaminases this elevated. For more information, see https://www.hhs.gov/hepatitis/blog/2017/1/17/hbv-reactivation-during-hcv-treatmen t.html

parts.text: 4 reasons for a patient to have anti-HCV-Ab positive but HCV PCR negative.

questions.model_answer: 4 reasons for anti-HCV-Ab positive but HCV RNA (PCR) negative: (1) spontaneous clearance of prior HCV infection (resolved infection); (2) successful prior treatment with sustained virologic response (cure); (3) false-positive antibody test (e.g., low pretest probability population, autoimmune disease, hypergammaglobulinemia); (4) intermittent/low-level viremia below the assay's limit of detection at the time of testing (test during a transient low point, or very early window before RNA becomes detectable is less likely given positive Ab - but intermittent viremia is an accepted mechanism).

questions.question: A man is referred to you with a new serological diagnosis of HCV. He is HIV negative and never traveled outside of North America. He has no evidence of cirrhosis.

parts.text: Name two microbiology tests you could do to guide management.
What is most likely genotype?
Based on the above answer, name 3 interferon-free treatment options and duration. Name each agent in the regimens.

questions.model_answer:
a) Two microbiology/virology tests to guide management: (1) HCV genotype (and subtype) testing, (2) quantitative HCV RNA (viral load).
b) Most likely genotype in a North American patient never travelling abroad: genotype 1a.
c) 3 interferon-free (DAA) options and durations for genotype 1a, non-cirrhotic, treatment-naive: (1) glecaprevir/pibrentasvir x 8 weeks; (2) sofosbuvir/velpatasvir x 12 weeks; (3) ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni) x 12 weeks (8 weeks if baseline HCV RNA <6 million IU/mL and select other criteria).

questions.question: HCV

parts.text: who should you screen, list 4.
Most common genotype?
List 2 DAAs (generic) that can treat that genotype?

questions.model_answer:
a) 4 groups to screen for HCV: (1) people who inject/have injected drugs (even once); (2) individuals born 1945-1975 (baby boomer cohort, one-time screen); (3) recipients of blood products/transfusion or organ transplant before 1992 (or from a country with inadequate screening); (4) HIV-positive individuals and men who have sex with men with high-risk sexual behaviour (also: infants born to HCV-infected mothers, healthcare workers with needlestick exposure).
b) Most common genotype (in North America): genotype 1a.
c) 2 DAAs (generic names) to treat genotype 1: (1) glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, (2) sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (ledipasvir/sofosbuvir also acceptable).

parts.text: Name 4 regimens - including duration - to treat hepatitis C in a patient who is treatment naive, non-cirrhotic, genotype 1a with no known resistance.

questions.model_answer: 4 regimens with duration for treatment-naive, non-cirrhotic genotype 1a, no known resistance: (1) glecaprevir/pibrentasvir x 8 weeks; (2) sofosbuvir/velpatasvir x 12 weeks; (3) ledipasvir/sofosbuvir x 12 weeks (or 8 weeks if HCV RNA <6 million IU/mL); (4) elbasvir/grazoprevir x 12 weeks (requires baseline NS5A resistance testing for genotype 1a, but stated no known resistance here).

questions.question: Newly diagnosed HCV. HIV (-). 2018 guidelines.

parts.text: What are 2 labs to help you manage this patient?
What is the most likely genotype?
What are 3-interferon free regimens?

cohort_answer.text: Labs: Viral load; genotype. Pretreatment evaluation should include risk factors for viral acquisition, signs/symptoms of advanced liver disease or extrahepatic manifestations, cofactors accelerating disease progression (alcohol, obesity, coinfections). Necessary labs: HCV RNA viral load, HCV genotype, liver biochemistry and function, abdominal ultrasound, fibrosis stage assessment, and tests to rule out HBV and HIV coinfection. || Genotype 1a most likely. Genotype 1 infection is the most prevalent genotype in Canada (65% of infected individuals: 56% genotype 1a, 33% genotype 1b, 10% unspecified/mixed). Genotypes 2 and 3 account for ~14% and 20% respectively; genotypes 4, 5, 6 very rare (<1%). (Myers et al., Canadian Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2015) || Interferon-free regimens: Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Maviret) x 8 weeks; Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni) x 12 weeks; Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa) x 12 weeks. (Buvir = NS5B polymerase inhibitor; Asvir = NS5A replication complex inhibitor; Previr = NS3 protease inhibitor)

questions.question: Hep C

parts.text: List 2 Pangenotypic drugs/regimens for HCV
Pick one of the regimens you described above and list the mechanism of action of each of its drug component -
One you would use in decompensated cirrhosis

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 pangenotypic regimens/drugs: (1) sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, (2) glecaprevir/pibrentasvir.
b) Mechanism of action of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir components: sofosbuvir is a nucleotide analogue prodrug that is metabolized intracellularly to its active triphosphate form, which inhibits the HCV NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, causing chain termination; velpatasvir is an NS5A inhibitor that blocks NS5A protein function, disrupting viral RNA replication and virion assembly.
c) Regimen usable in decompensated cirrhosis: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (with ribavirin) - protease inhibitor-containing regimens (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, elbasvir/grazoprevir, ledipasvir/sofosbuvir with a PI) are contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis.

parts.text: Complete the table for the 3 DAA regimens
b) State one additional test you would need to order for 1 regimen

cohort_answer.text:
Sofosbuvir-Ledipasvir: 12 weeks, ribavirin yes if decompensated/no if compensated, increases TDF concentrations, ≥97% cure rate. Ombitasvir-Paritaprevir/r: not recommended if decompensated, reduced anti-Hep C concentrations from CYP3A4 inducers. Sofosbuvir-simeprevir: not recommended if decompensated, reduced simeprevir concentrations from CYP3A4 inducers. Not recommended to use Maviret or Epclusa with Efavirenz. (Additional regimen details: Harvoni x12wk, Epclusa x12wk, Maviret x8wk, Vosevi x12wk salvage)

questions.question: Hep C Table. Patient with compensated cirrhosis, Genotype 1a Hep C. Needs treatment. Has HIV on truvada/efavirenz.

parts.text: Drugs (Harvoni, Simep+Sofos, Ombitasvir/Paritipravir/Dasabuvir + Ritonavir) on Y-axis. On X-axis – Duration of tx, need for ribavirin, drug drug interactions.
Last question – what is viral test needed if patient to start simeptravir/sofos.

questions.model_answer:
a) For compensated cirrhosis, genotype 1a, on tenofovir/emtricitabine/efavirenz for HIV: Harvoni (ledipasvir/sofosbuvir) x 12 weeks, no ribavirin needed, but efavirenz reduces ledipasvir levels - significant interaction requiring caution/avoidance if possible. Simeprevir/sofosbuvir: not recommended in genotype 1a with cirrhosis due to Q80K resistance concerns and significant interaction - efavirenz substantially reduces simeprevir levels (contraindicated combination). Ombitasvir/paritaprevir/dasabuvir/ritonavir (Viekira): contraindicated with efavirenz (major CYP3A4 interaction via ritonavir boosting) and not recommended in cirrhosis without ribavirin dose adjustment; requires ribavirin in genotype 1a.
b) Viral test needed before starting simeprevir/sofosbuvir: NS3 Q80K polymorphism testing (associated with reduced response to simeprevir in genotype 1a).

questions.question: Hepatitis C treatment

parts.text: List 2 treatment regimen that would treat all genotypes
For one of the regimen above, describe mechanism of action for each component
Which do you recommend for a person with decompensated cirrhosis

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: Epclusa (Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir); Maviret (Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir); Vosevi (Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir/Voxilaprevir) - direct acting antiviral, failures only. Mechanisms - Epclusa: Sofosbuvir - uridine nucleoside inhibitor of HCV NS5B Polymerase (directly acting antiviral), prodrug metabolized to uridine nucleoside triphosphate, chain termination; Velpatasvir - NS5A inhibitor (binds to NS5A protein, blocks ability to regulate replication through unclear mechanism). Maviret: Glecaprevir - Protease inhibitor; Pibrentasvir - NS5A inhibitor. Vosevi: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (see Epclusa); Voxilaprevir - Protease inhibitor. Decompensated cirrhosis: All protease inhibitors are contraindicated so would choose Epclusa plus ribavirin; if MELD >15-18 patient may benefit from deferral of therapy

questions.question: Hep C in pregnancy

parts.text: Rate of vertical transmission from mother with chronic hep C
2 diagnostic tests for the infant, and when is the appropriate timing to use them

questions.model_answer:
a) Rate of vertical transmission from a mother with chronic HCV: approximately 5-6% (Mandell text cites a range of 0-4% across large studies; commonly quoted figure overall is about 5-6%, higher with HIV coinfection).
b) 2 diagnostic tests for the infant and timing: (1) HCV RNA (PCR) testing, which can be performed at 2-6 months of age (avoids the window of detectable maternal antibody interference and can identify early infection); (2) HCV antibody testing performed after 18 months of age (once passively transferred maternal antibody has cleared, a positive result reflects the infant's own infection).

questions.question: Q33 (2023, AM). Hep C in pregnant mom (not co-infected). (PREGNANCY)

parts.text: Risk % of vertical transmission
2 diagnostic tests for baby and best time to do them

cohort_answer.text:
Risk of vertical transmission: HCV monoinfection 5-6%; HCV+HIV coinfection 10-11%.
2 diagnostic tests for baby and timing: Perinatal diagnosis - HCV RNA on 2 occasions (at 2 months and 6 months) OR HCV Antibody at 18 months (will have cleared maternal antibodies). 20-30% of babies will clear infection by age 2-3 years old. AASLD and IDSA recommend treatment for all children >3 years (CPS).

parts.text: Risk of transmission of HCV?

cohort_answer.text: Recent systematic review demonstrated a vertical transmission rate of 5.8% (95% CI 4.2-7.8) from HCV-infected mothers without HIV co-infection, and 10.8% (95% CI 7.6-15.2) with sub-optimally controlled HIV co-infection. ~10% in mothers with HIV and Hep C co-infection; 5-6% in mothers with Hep C mono-infection

questions.question: HCV and HIV at 18 weeks gestation

parts.text: Risk of transmission of HCV?
Need to quantify viral load (PCR) at this point?
Safe to breastfeed?
How should the mother deliver the baby
How should the baby be tested and followed for HCV?

cohort_answer.text: A) HCV monoinfection: 5-6%; HCV+HIV Coinfection: 10-11%. Risk factors for vertical transmission of HCV: HIV co-infection, viremia, peripheral blood mononuclear cell infection, maternal IVDU. Not risk factors: genotype, breastfeeding, mode of delivery. B) Not needed for Hep C - no safety/efficacy data for treatment to prevent MTCT. Viral load rises during 3rd trimester and drops post-partum, some moms may even clear HCV postpartum. Manage HIV (including quantifying VL and treating). C) Yes for HCV, not safe for HIV, unless nipples cracked/bleeding. D) Any mode of delivery is fine for HCV; avoid obstetrical/fetal procedures, avoid prolonged ROM. C/S preferred for HIV if VL>1000 or unknown at time of delivery. E) HCV serology at 12-18 months (maternal antibodies should have cleared by now). If negative: no follow up needed. If positive: check HCV RNA - if negative: falsely positive antibody; if positive: infected. If significant parental anxiety can do PCR testing at 2 months (no earlier, not sensitive) with serologic follow up as above. If baby confirmed HCV+: genotype, check HBV, HIV, LFTs. Treatment: Age>12y: Genotype 1,4,5,6 - Harvoni (Ledipasvir-sofosbuvir) 12 weeks (24 weeks if cirrhosis); Genotype 2,3 - Epclusa (velpatasvir-sofosbuvir) vs sofosbuvir+RBV; all genotypes - glecaprevir-pibrentasvir 8 weeks, with cirrhosis 12 weeks. Age<12y: wait till 12y, referral to center with expertise in pediatric Hep C, treat once drugs available with approval in this age group.

Patient with compensated cirrhosis, Genotype 1a Hep C. Needs treatment. Has HIV on truvada/efavirenz.

parts.text: Last question - what is viral test needed if patient to start simeprevir/sofosbuvir.

cohort_answer.text: Check for Q80K polymorphism, confers low level resistance to in vitro simeprevir activity. If the patient is NON-CIRRHOTIC -> this does not matter. Can treat for 12 weeks. If the patient is CIRRHOTIC and Q80K polymorphism present, consider a different regimen. As a rule -> if patient has cirrhosis, we have to check for resistance. parts.text: A. 4 (or 6) reasons (ie. Clinical scenarios) to test for Hep C RNA (either qualitative or quantitative)
Most important prognostic factor in treatment of Hep C
C. List 4 modes of transmission/acquisition.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Positive Ab - Active HCV infection (confirm diagnosis during clinical disease, post-exposure); Post-Treatment (look for response, sustained virologic response); Re-exposure after cure. Negative/Unreliable Ab - Vertical transmission (infant during first 18 months, serology unreliable due to maternal antibodies, use RNA instead); Immunosuppressed Patients (hemodialysis, transplant recipients, advanced HIV - high rate of false negative Ab, RNA should be done regardless of antibody results); Acute hepatitis or Recent exposure (if high clinical suspicion, perform RNA as it may be detectable prior to reactive antibodies; Ab takes 2-6 months after exposure to develop); Concern for transmissibility e.g. deceased donor organ transplantation or needle stick origin, need result quickly

Most important prognostic factor: Presence of cirrhosis - restricts certain drugs, predicts overall mortality and need for transplant, HCC only occurs in those with cirrhosis with Hep C (unlike Hep B)

C: Vertical transmission. Parenteral transmission (Blood transfusion, IVDU, needlestick). Nosocomial transmission (unsafe medical practices). Transplant. Sexual transmission

parts.text: Name 6 different viruses that cause cancer and what type of cancer?

questions.model_answer: (1) Human papillomavirus (HPV) - cervical, anal, vulvar/vaginal/penile, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. (2) Hepatitis B virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (3) Hepatitis C virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (4) Epstein-Barr virus - Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma. (5) Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8/KSHV) - Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease. (6) Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) - adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (Merkel cell polyomavirus causing Merkel cell carcinoma is another acceptable answer).
